newsitem.title: UK: Dollar ends more than 2-1/2 yen higher in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends more than 2-1/2 yen higher in Europe.

text.p: The dollar ended more than 2-1/2 yen higher in Europe as Japanese officials dampened speculation of a rise in Japanese interest rates and played down signs of friction with the U.S. about its growing trade surpluses.
Comments in Tokyo from senior Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara were the trigger for an overnight dollar/yen surge of up to four percent.

Sakakibara, believed to be orchestrator of Japanese foreign exchange policy, said the U.S./Japan trade spat was being played up excessively. He was also quoted as saying it is unlikely Japan's interest rates will be raised soon.

"You need a pretty strong stomach to the play the dollar/yen market right now but we think the worst is probably over," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets. "I would expect the dollar to be a buy on dips from here and to grind higher again."

At 1530 GMT, the dollar was trading at 113.94/04 yen compared with 111.20/25 late Wednesday and a seven-month low at 110.52 set Wednesday. Just six weeks ago, dollar/yen set its highest level since August 1992.
The dollar gave up some of its early gains in Europe later as concerns about the U.S. response persisted.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin repeated recent comments that a sustained rise in Japan's trade surplus could hurt global growth and spark a protectionist backlash in the U.S..
However, Rubin said there was no sign yet the rise in the surplus will be sustained, He said U.S. dollar policy was unchanged and the rate will never be used it as a trade tool.
Rubin said Japan's trade surplus was not on the agenda of the Group of Seven summit in Denver later this month but he expected a discussion on the recent volatility in the foreign exchanges.
U.S. Trade Undersecretary Lawrence Summers is due to speak later at 1800 GMT.

"The Japanese surplus has not yet approached critical proportions, interest rates there are likely to be on hold for a while yet and the U.S. can have no interest in reversing its exchange rate policy at this stage," said Stretch at NatWest.

The dollar was given further support earlier after the Organistaion of Economic Growth and Development in its latest report forecast a half-point rise in U.S. interest rates in the middle of this year.
While this raised speculation about a rise in U.S. rates at the Federal Reserve's policy-making meeting on July 1-2, soft U.S. retail sales data later in the day clouded the issue.
April sales unexpectedly fell 0.1 percent during the month.
Dollar/mark was buoyed above 1.72, meantime, as the mark continued to give back gains made earlier in the week on a bout of jitters about preparations for European monetary union.
Tensions have eased as the German government is expected acquiesce to demands from the new French administration to include a committment to employment in the review of the Maastricht Treaty.
German and French leaders meet tomorrow in the French town of Poitiers for their regular bilateral summit ahead of the Amsterdam summit of European Union leaders on Monday.
"The seeds of a compromise are already there," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan.
"It looks as if the Germans are prepared to accept a slightly softer path toward EMU, in terms of criteria definitions etc., in exchange for a hard EMU after 1999 with the stability pact intact."

Persaud said the inclusion of a jobs pact alongside the stability pact will be as appealing to German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, heading for re-election next year, as it appears to be for the new French socialist government.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
